description: Active Future Labs is a collaborative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, bringing together interests in computer science, data science and software development. Our focus is on using NASA Earth observation data, Python and statistical analysis to investigate environmental trends and communicate meaningful insights through interactive visualisations. We aim to combine technical innovation, scientific curiosity and creative problem-solving to address real-world challenges.
summary:
EARTHWATCH is an interactive environmental investigation platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps users explore how Earth systems are changing and how strong the statistical evidence is.

We combined monthly observations from NASA POWER, GLDAS, GPM IMERG and MERRA-2 across ten environmental variables and 360 defined study areas from 2000 to 2024. A Python analysis pipeline estimates long-term trends, accounts for seasonality and temporal dependence, and reports confidence intervals and adjusted significance tests. Our CesiumJS-powered globe brings these results together with searchable locations, environmental signal alerts, visualisations and detailed regional dossiers. An optional live service can analyse NASA POWER observations for user-selected coordinates.

EARTHWATCH addresses the Earth System Trend Detective challenge by helping people investigate what is changing, where changes occur, and how much confidence the available data supports. By translating complex measurements into accessible explanations while showing uncertainty and limitations, the platform supports environmental learning, exploratory research and evidence-based discussion.
details:
EARTHWATCH is an interactive Earth observation and statistical intelligence platform developed to investigate long-term environmental change. Our objective was to make complex environmental datasets more accessible while preserving the scientific rigour needed to distinguish meaningful trends from natural variability and uncertainty.

Rather than presenting static climate graphs, EARTHWATCH allows users to investigate environmental patterns through an interactive three-dimensional globe, searchable geographical locations, environmental signal feeds and detailed statistical reports.

Data and Methodology

The platform brings together observations from four NASA data services: POWER, GLDAS, GPM IMERG and MERRA-2.

We analyse ten environmental variables covering air temperature, precipitation, humidity, soil wetness, soil moisture, evaporation, runoff and atmospheric aerosols.

Our primary historical dataset covers January 2000 to December 2024 across 360 geographically defined study areas.

A Python data-processing pipeline retrieves, standardises and aggregates the observations, accounting for differences in data sources, units, geographical coverage and temporal resolution.

We use Ordinary Least Squares regression with seasonal controls and heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent standard errors to estimate trends over time. The analytical engine calculates changes per decade, confidence intervals and p-values, with Benjamini–Hochberg and Benjamini–Yekutieli corrections to address multiple comparisons.

Additional statistical and exploratory methods investigate changing environmental variability, differences between datasets and potential shifts in environmental conditions.

Interactive Features

EARTHWATCH transforms these analytical outputs into an interactive investigation experience.

Users can explore a CesiumJS-powered 3D globe, select environmental variables, search geographical locations and examine detailed regional dossiers. These reports combine time-series visualisations, estimated trends, statistical evidence and explanations written for non-specialist audiences.

An environmental signal detection system highlights locations exhibiting potentially meaningful changes in environmental conditions. Rather than treating every detected pattern as a confirmed discovery, the platform communicates the strength and limitations of the underlying evidence.

The application also includes a live Python API service capable of retrieving NASA POWER observations for user-selected geographical coordinates, complementing the pre-analysed historical archive.

Technologies

Our backend was developed using Python, including Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Statsmodels, xarray and FastAPI. SQLite supports local caching of NASA observations and statistical results.

The frontend uses JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Vite and CesiumJS to provide an interactive geospatial interface. NASA GIBS imagery provides the globe's Earth visualisation, while OpenStreetMap-based geocoding supports geographical searches.

Google Colab was used for data acquisition and scientific development, with GitHub supporting collaboration and version control.

Innovation and Impact

EARTHWATCH goes beyond conventional environmental dashboards by combining multiple NASA datasets with automated statistical analysis, environmental signal detection and accessible scientific explanations.

Its main contribution is connecting geographical visualisation with statistical evidence. Users can investigate not only where environmental changes appear to be occurring, but also how large those changes are and how confidently they can be interpreted.

Our intended audience includes students, educators, researchers and members of the public interested in understanding environmental change.

The project also recognises important limitations. Its geographical study areas are defined sampling boxes rather than complete administrative or ecological regions, while statistical findings remain subject to data coverage, model assumptions and uncertainty.

By making environmental observations easier to investigate and interpret, EARTHWATCH aims to encourage scientific curiosity, data literacy and more informed conversations about our changing planet.

Source Code & Documentation

The complete EARTHWATCH source code, statistical analysis pipeline, processed historical datasets, development documentation and version history are publicly available at https://github.com/skandermian/active-future-labs.
